clue.text: A U-boat, to begin with, has never exploded in German transport lanes

indicators.note: to begin with points at the opening letter of each of the two words that follow, has and never
something exploded is blown apart, so the gathered letters fly into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, without the hyphen
the first letters of has and never

explanation.surface: A wartime submarine has never been blown up on a German road, an oddly mixed picture of sea and land.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is A, the whole of U-boat, and the opening letters of has never, shuffled together into AUTOBAHN.
explanation.definitionFit: An autobahn is a German motorway, a high-speed road with several traffic lanes in each direction.

clue.text: Set up in first pad, adolescent achieves accommodation

indicators.note: in says the letters wanted sit inside the run of words that follows
in a down clue, set up means lifted upwards, so the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters running across the end of first, all of pad and the start of adolescent

explanation.surface: A teenager settling into a first flat finds somewhere to live.
explanation.walkthrough: Accommodation looks like housing for the adolescent in a first pad, but here it means adjustment, as in making accommodations.
explanation.definitionFit: To accommodate oneself is to adjust to new circumstances, so someone who achieves accommodation adjusts and fits in.

clue.text: Beckett character turns up, carrying finally, finally a tiny pooch

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up flips the name so it reads from the bottom upwards
the first finally asks for the closing letter of the word placed after it
carrying means holding something inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the never-arriving figure in Samuel Beckett's play Waiting for Godot
the last letter of the second finally

explanation.surface: A character from Beckett finally shows up at last, carrying a little dog.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that Godot, famous for never turning up, turns up here. The repeated word is one indicator and one source of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A toy dog is a breed kept very small, such as a Chihuahua, so it is a tiny pooch or pet.

clue.text: In audition, smile I supposed to be welcoming expression

indicators.note: an audition is a hearing, so the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

blocks.note: smile is beam, I stays I, and supposed is guessed

explanation.surface: An actor at an audition smiles, guessing that a warm phrase is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying be my guest grants someone permission or invites them in, a polite phrase of hospitality and welcome.

clue.text: Foal had idly relaxed in hay for time off

indicators.note: relaxed suggests loosened up, so the preceding letters fall out of order
in places the rearranged letters inside the word after it

blocks.note: these eleven letters rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young horse lazes about in the hay, taking a break.
explanation.definitionFit: A half-day holiday is an afternoon or morning off work or school, a short period of leisure.

clue.text: Ancient vessel emptied, filled with fizzy wine

indicators.note: an emptied vessel has lost its contents, so only its outer letters remain
filled with means something is put inside the emptied shell

blocks.note: a pot is a vessel
Asti is a sparkling Italian wine

explanation.surface: An old vessel is emptied out and refilled with sparkling wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Ancient looks like it describes the vessel, but it is the definition, used jokily of a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone past it is too old to do what they once could, an informal way of calling a person over the hill.

clue.text: Primarily, annoyed, narked, getting extremely ratty?

definitions.text: Primarily, annoyed, narked, getting extremely ratty?

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so the opening letters of the next three words are kept
extremely means at the extremes, so only the two outside letters of the next word count

blocks.note: the first letters of annoyed, narked and getting
the first and last letters of ratty

explanation.surface: Someone first annoyed, then narked, ends up very ratty.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: the letters come from the words, and the words together describe the answer. Ratty is British slang for irritable.
explanation.definitionFit: Being annoyed and narked and ratty all describe someone cross, a state of irritation building into temper.

clue.text: ‘Where to drink, Everyman?’ (Everyman, at last, answers.) ‘When to drink?’

indicators.note: at last means at the very end, so only the closing letter of the word after it is kept

blocks.note: a baby or young animal drinks its milk from a teat
the setter speaking of himself is I
the setter again, this time as me
the last letter of answers

explanation.surface: A little dialogue in which the setter is asked where to go for a drink and finally answers with a question about when.
explanation.walkthrough: Where to drink suggests a pub, but it is a teat, where a baby feeds. Everyman appears twice, giving both I and ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Teatimes are the customary afternoon hours for taking tea, so they are moments one sits down for a cuppa.

clue.text: To start with, Nicomachus died in his home with painful sickness

indicators.note: to start with asks for only the opening letter of the name after it
in places the preceding letters inside the place named next

blocks.note: Nicomachus of Thebes was an ancient Greek painter, so his home city is Thebes
the first letter of Nicomachus
D is the standard abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek, Nicomachus, dies at home of a painful illness.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a classical obituary; his home has to be identified as Thebes, the Greek city.
explanation.definitionFit: The bends is decompression sickness, which strikes divers who surface too fast, causing severe joint pain.

clue.text: Army officers diverted stream in regions

indicators.note: a diverted stream is sent off its course, so its letters are rerouted
in puts the rearranged letters inside the word that follows

blocks.note: the six letters rearranged
quarters are districts or regions of a town

explanation.surface: Army officers redirect a stream through a district, an engineering job.
explanation.definitionFit: Quartermasters are military officers responsible for supplies, rations and accommodation for their troops.

clue.text: Horrible baby’s malodorous sample

indicators.note: a sample is a small portion taken from something, so the letters are a slice of the words before

blocks.note: the run of letters from inside baby's and the start of malodorous

explanation.surface: A smelly sample from a baby, as nappy-changing parents know, is truly horrible.
explanation.definitionFit: Abysmal means appallingly bad or dreadful, the very depths of poor quality, close in sense to awful.

clue.text: You finally admitting dead pager’s broken? Perhaps get a new phone

indicators.note: finally keeps only the closing letter of the word before it
a broken device is in pieces, so the letters of the word before are jumbled
admitting means letting in, so one letter is placed inside the others

blocks.note: the last letter of you
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for dead

explanation.surface: Your old pager is dead and broken, so maybe it is time for a new phone.
explanation.definitionFit: To upgrade is to replace something with a better model, and getting a new mobile is the typical example, hence perhaps.

clue.text: Piece of cloth on goolies?

indicators.note: piece of means a fragment taken from what follows, so the letters lie within the next words

blocks.note: the run of letters at the end of cloth, all of on and the start of goolies

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about a bit of fabric worn over one's private parts.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the hiding place and the description. Goolies is British slang for testicles.
explanation.definitionFit: This skimpy undergarment or swimsuit barely covers the groin, held by a narrow strip, so it is a scrap of fabric worn there.

clue.text: Tired, I cry about trendy street food

indicators.note: about suggests turning round and around, so the words before are rearranged

blocks.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone worn out weeps over fashionable food bought from a stall.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirty rice is a Cajun dish of rice cooked with chicken livers and spices, now popular at food stalls and markets.

clue.text: Dean’s address is, surprisingly, never ever dry

indicators.note: surprisingly hints at something unexpected, so the words after it come out in an unexpected order

blocks.note: the twelve letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cathedral dean's speech, surprisingly, is never ever dull, or perhaps the dean is never sober.
explanation.walkthrough: Address looks like a speech or a home, but it is the formal title used for a dean.
explanation.definitionFit: The Very Reverend is the honorific style for a dean of a cathedral in the Church of England, used when addressing one.

clue.text: Poet represented azure pond

indicators.note: represented means presented again in another form, so the next words are reshaped

blocks.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A poet depicts a blue pond in verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Ezra Pound was an American modernist writer of verse, author of The Cantos, so he is a famous poet.

clue.text: Prepare for fight … or settle

blocks.note: first meaning: take a boxer's stance, ready to trade blows
second meaning: pay off what is owed, clearing a debt

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis and or make it sound like a choice between brawling and backing down; they are two meanings of one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both adopting a fighting posture against someone and paying what you owe to settle accounts.

clue.text: Merit given by the Queen to traitor

indicators.note: given by suggests something handed over alongside, so one piece is followed by the other

blocks.note: desert in the sense of what one deserves, as in just deserts
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: The monarch hands out an honour to someone who betrayed the country.
explanation.walkthrough: Merit hides the noun desert, meaning what you deserve, as in getting your just deserts.
explanation.definitionFit: A deserter abandons their army or cause, so betrays comrades, making them a turncoat or traitor.

clue.text: ‘Quakerism’ … not ‘quaking’ … ?

indicators.note: quaking means shaking, so the letters of the words around it are shaken up

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzled query as to whether Quakerism is about quaking, which is how the Quakers got their name.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the punctuation mark that ends the clue; the ellipses make not look like a contradiction.
explanation.definitionFit: The final symbol of the clue is itself the punctuation sign written at the end of a query.

clue.text: Cockney bruiser returns to wasteland

indicators.note: returns means goes back, so the letters are read in the backwards direction

blocks.note: a bruiser is a hard nut, and a Cockney drops the H of hard

explanation.surface: A London tough guy goes back to some barren ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the working-class East London accent, known for dropping the initial H.
explanation.definitionFit: Tundra is the vast treeless Arctic plain with frozen subsoil, a cold barren region or wasteland.

clue.text: Dates and locations for actions

blocks.note: first meaning: goes out with romantically, woos
second meaning: places where lawsuits are heard

explanation.walkthrough: Dates and locations sound like a schedule of times and places; actions here are legal cases.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means wooing a partner and also the halls of justice where legal suits are tried.

clue.text: If parties needing animation, drinks served beforehand

indicators.note: something needing animation must be stirred into life, so the words before are stirred up

blocks.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: If a party needs livening up, hand out some drinks first.
explanation.definitionFit: Aperitifs are alcoholic drinks taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite, served ahead of dinner.

clue.text: Nooky after pub: do you agree?

indicators.note: after places the first-named piece behind the second-named one

blocks.note: an inn is a pub
it is slang for sex, as is nooky

explanation.surface: A bit of slap and tickle after the pub: are you up for it?
explanation.walkthrough: Innit is a British slang tag, short for isn't it, tacked on to seek agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: The tag question asks the listener to confirm a remark, as in isn't that so, inviting assent.

clue.text: Hellish character, government by the wealthy? Not half

indicators.note: not half means only half survives, so the back half of the term is cut off

blocks.note: rule by the rich is plutocracy

explanation.surface: A fiendish figure rules for the rich, or not quite.
explanation.walkthrough: Not half is also British slang for very much, which pulls the eye away from its role as a cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Pluto was the Roman god of the underworld, ruler of Hades, so a figure from hell.

clue.text: Country song I Eat Bananas lacking gravity

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so the named letter is taken away
bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
g is the symbol for acceleration due to gravity

explanation.surface: A national song with the silly title I Eat Bananas, which has no gravitas.
explanation.walkthrough: Bananas looks like part of the song title, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonia is a Baltic nation in northern Europe, with Tallinn as its capital.

clue.text: Country dancing rodeo mostly welcoming cougar, oddly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
dancing letters move about and change places
oddly picks the letters in odd positions, first, third and fifth
welcoming means taking in a guest, so one group goes inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the first, third and fifth letters of cougar

explanation.surface: A national dance at a rodeo makes room for a big cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecuador is a South American nation on the equator, with Quito as its capital.

clue.text: Knock off turbulent priest beforehand

indicators.note: beforehand means coming earlier, so one piece is placed in front of the other

blocks.note: P is an abbreviation for priest
turbulent in the sense of stormy, wild with anger

explanation.surface: An echo of Henry II's who will rid me of this turbulent priest, asking someone to bump off Becket.
explanation.walkthrough: Knock off suggests murder here, but it means copy illegally.
explanation.definitionFit: To pirate is to copy and sell goods illegally, and knock off is slang for making a cheap counterfeit.

clue.text: Rovers maybe making itinerant crusades

indicators.note: itinerant means wandering about, so the letters roam into a new order

blocks.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Wanderers make roaming crusades.
explanation.walkthrough: Rovers looks like wanderers, matching itinerant, but Rover is a British car make, so second-hand Rovers are examples.
explanation.definitionFit: Rover was a British motor manufacturer, so old Rovers on a forecourt are an example of second-hand vehicles.
